strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: the paper systematically explores SFT data scaling (200k–2.8M) to establish the plateau claim before applying RL, which is a good methodological practice that isolates the true contribution of RL from unsaturated-baseline effects.

Strong state-of-the-art results: MSRL achieves the best open-source performance on ChartMimic (96.5 exec rate, 83.8 high-level) and ReachQA, surpassing the previous chart-specific SOTA (ChartCoder) by clear margins and rivaling GPT-4o.

Well-designed multi-granularity reward: combining rule-based textual rewards (code normalization, soft value matching, execution) with a render-and-compare visual reward from an MLLM judge is a sensible and complete reward design for structured-output generation.

Good ablation coverage: the paper ablates SFT vs RL stages, textual vs visual vs hybrid rewards (Table 4), and one-stage vs two-stage RL schedules (Table 5), and includes reward-trajectory plots (Figures 3-4) that provide insight into training dynamics.
Large-scale, more realistic data pipeline: constructing 3M chart-code pairs from real arXiv tables with multi-stage filtering addresses the known weakness of simplistic synthetic chart corpora.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core components (GRPO, rule-based RLVR, render-and-compare visual feedback with an MLLM judge) are each established; the contribution is primarily their combination and careful tuning in the chart-to-code domain, e.g., closely related to Chen et al. (2025b) and Chart-R1 (2025a).

Potential test-set contamination is not addressed: the training corpus is built from arXiv paper charts, and benchmarks like ChartMimic are also derived from real paper figures; without an overlap/deduplication analysis, the SOTA gains could be partly inflated by distributional overlap or even near-duplicates.

Bias in the visual reward: the MLLM judge (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) is from the same model family as the policy model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), creating a potential reward-hacking/self-preference bias, and no validation of judge quality (e.g., correlation with human judgment) is provided.

The plateau conclusion is weakly supported: it rests on a single base model, a single training configuration (one epoch, fixed hyperparameters), and only six data-scale points without variance or significance analysis; alternative explanations (e.g., capacity limits vs. data diversity limits) are not disentangled.

Gains of the two-stage curriculum are small (e.g., 78.06 to 78.62 low-level on ChartMimic) and some ablation settings are within noise; no statistical significance tests or multiple seeds are reported.

Some results are surprising and under-explained: the MSRL-SFT model already jumps from Qwen2.5-VL-7B's 44.6 to 73.0 low-level on ChartMimic, and the ablation Table 4 shows single-stage hybrid rewards can underperform textual-only on execution rate, warranting deeper analysis.

Missing details hurt reproducibility: reward weights are stated but the code-normalization procedure, exact prompts for the visual judge, and filtering criteria are only sketched; the 'Project:' link is empty, so no code or dataset release is evident for a 3M-pair corpus that is one of the main claimed contributions.
Figures 3-4 are hard to read at the provided resolution and the paper has minor presentation issues (e.g., 'Axriv' typo in Figure 2, duplicated MM-EUREKA reference).

strengths: Systematic empirical study of the SFT data-scaling plateau in chart-to-code generation, backed by a large 3M-pair training corpus built from real-world arXiv tables, which isolates the true effect of RL from gains that merely compensate for an undertrained SFT baseline.
Comprehensive ablation studies (SFT/RL interplay, reward composition, two-stage curriculum in Tables 3-5) that credibly support the two-stage textual-then-hybrid reward design.

Strong and consistent empirical results: new open-source SOTA on ChartMimic and ReachQA (e.g., 96.5/78.6/83.8 on ChartMimic), with gains over the saturated SFT model (+6.2 high-level) and parity with GPT-4o in several low-level metrics.
Reasonable and mostly reproducible implementation reporting (GPU hours, learning rates, rollout counts, reward weights, evaluation protocols and corrected ChartCoder numbers).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the recipe is a fairly standard combination of GRPO + rule-based verifiable rewards + an MLLM-as-judge render-and-compare reward; visual/rendering-based rewards for chart-to-code already appear in prior work (e.g., Chen et al. 2025b), so the contribution is largely an engineering integration rather than a new technique.

The 'SFT plateau' finding is expected and not surprising, and the plateau is demonstrated on a single model family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and a single task; the paper's framing oversells this as a central contribution.

Potential evaluator bias and reward hacking are unaddressed: the visual reward uses Qwen2.5-VL-72B, from the same model family as the trained policy, and the paper provides no analysis of whether the MLLM judge can be gamed, no correlation between visual reward and human judgment, and no robustness study of judge sensitivity.

Possible train/test contamination is not discussed: training data is curated from arXiv tables while ChartMimic examples also derive from real academic charts; no de-duplication or overlap check between the 3M training corpus and the two evaluation benchmarks is reported.

Hyperparameter choices (reward weights w_t, w_v, w_e, per-component weights, ±5% tolerance) are stated without justification or sensitivity analysis; the ±5% soft matching tolerance in particular could materially affect rewards.
No release of the 3M-pair corpus, RL dataset, or code (the project link on page 1 is empty), which weakens reproducibility and the claimed value of the dataset contribution.

Scope of evaluation is narrow: only ChartMimic Direct Mimic and ReachQA plotting scripts; no generalization test to other structured-output or chart benchmarks, and no error analysis of remaining failures.

Presentation issues: Table 3's rows are unlabeled (baseline vs. SFT vs. RL vs. SFT+RL must be inferred), Figure 2 is dense and hard to parse, and the abstract/introduction claims (e.g., 'significantly outperforms all methods in the chart domain') occasionally overstate what is shown given the corrected ChartCoder numbers are close in execution rate.

strengths: The paper presents a comprehensive empirical study of the SFT scaling plateau in chart-to-code generation, with experiments at six data scales (200k–2.8M), which is a useful and clearly presented contribution to understanding when SFT saturates for structured-output multimodal tasks.

A very large training corpus (3M chart-code pairs) built from real-world arXiv tables rather than purely synthetic patterns, with a sensible two-stage filtering pipeline for curating the 33k RL subset; this is the largest chart-to-code corpus to date and is a concrete resource contribution.

The MSRL method is well-motivated: the multi-granularity reward (rule-based textual rewards across five dimensions plus a render-and-compare visual reward from an MLLM judge) addresses a genuine limitation of purely textual RLVR rewards for chart fidelity.

Strong empirical results: new SOTA among open-source models on ChartMimic (96.5 exec rate, 83.8 high-level) and ReachQA, surpassing GPT-4o on several metrics with a 7B model, supported by reasonably thorough ablations (SFT/RL interplay, reward ablation, two-stage curriculum ablation).

The ablation isolating RL gains on a saturated SFT baseline is a thoughtful experimental design choice that strengthens the central claim that RL breaks the SFT plateau rather than merely compensating for under-trained SFT.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method combines well-established components (GRPO/RLVR, rule-based rewards, render-and-compare MLLM-judge visual feedback, curriculum RL); the contribution is primarily an engineering integration applied to one task rather than a new technique.

The visual reward depends on a Qwen2.5-VL-72B judge scoring outputs from a Qwen2.5-VL-7B policy, raising concerns about judge bias and reward hacking (e.g., optimizing the judge's scoring function rather than true visual fidelity); the paper does not analyze reward-hacking behavior, judge robustness, or correlation between visual reward and human judgments.

Reward ablation results are mixed: Table 4 shows the combined textual+visual reward underperforms the textual-only reward on execution rate (96.33 vs 97.00) and Table 5's gains over single-stage settings are small (~0.2–1.4 points), so the necessity of the visual reward and two-stage curriculum is not decisively demonstrated.
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or repeated runs; several claimed improvements are within a range where training variance could matter.

Generalization concerns: experiments use a single base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and only two chart benchmarks; no evidence the plateau finding or MSRL transfers to other models, scales, or adjacent structured-output tasks (e.g., Web2Code, Plot2Code).

Reproducibility is unclear: the 'Project' link is empty, the dataset release status is not stated, and data generation depends on closed models (Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4.1-mini) and GPT-4o/GPT-4V evaluations, all of which complicate exact reproduction; no discussion of potential benchmark contamination from LLM-generated training data.
Hyperparameter choices (reward weights, ±5% soft-matching tolerance, stage data splits) are reported but not justified or sensitized; ablation over these design choices is missing.

Writing issues: the notation w_t is overloaded between the total reward weight and the title/subtitle reward weight in Eq. 1 vs. Section 4.2, duplicated references (Meng et al. 2025a/b), and several typos (e.g., 'Axriv').

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: the paper systematically varies SFT data scale (200k to 2.8M) to establish a saturated SFT baseline, cleanly demonstrating the SFT plateau before applying RL — this is a more rigorous methodology than prior chart-to-code works that apply RL directly after weak SFT baselines.

Strong and convincing results: MSRL achieves clear SOTA among open-source models on ChartMimic (96.5 Exec, 83.8 High-Level) and ReachQA, rivaling GPT-4o, with consistent gains across low-level metrics in Table 3.

The 3M-pair dataset built from real arXiv tables addresses a genuine limitation of prior purely synthetic corpora, with a sensible two-stage curation pipeline and favorable dataset comparisons in Table 1 and Table D.

Unusually thorough ablations: SFT/RL interplay (Table 4), single- vs two-stage reward strategies with GPU-hour cost accounting (Table 5), visual evaluator selection with human-score correlation analysis (Figure A, Table B), GRPO vs DPO (Table C), and out-of-domain generalization to Seaborn/Plotly (Table 6).
Good reproducibility posture: implementation details (hyperparameters, reward weights, GPU hours, frameworks) and exact prompt templates are provided, and the supplementary code is included.
weaknesses: Moderate conceptual novelty: combining rule-based textual rewards with rendering-based visual (LLM-judge) rewards and GRPO is an assembly of existing techniques (RLVR, LLM-as-judge visual feedback, rendering-aware RL as in Rodriguez et al. 2025b and Gu et al. 2025). The primary contribution is empirical/engineering rather than a new method or insight.

Potential circularity/bias in the visual reward: the judge (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) and the base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) come from the same model family. While evaluator ablations help, reward hacking risks of an LLM judge during RL optimization are analyzed only statically (score correlation on 200 samples), not during training.
Missing technical detail on the code normalization step, which is claimed as key to making textual rewards robust — no algorithm, coverage statistics, or failure analysis is provided.

Train/test contamination risk is only partially mitigated: using arXiv papers from 2023 and earlier reduces but does not eliminate overlap with ChartMimic (e.g., charts reproduced in papers before the cutoff), and no deduplication check against test benchmarks is reported.

Some claims are under-supported: the mechanistic explanation for the SFT plateau (uniform token weighting vs. infrequent critical tokens) is asserted but not experimentally isolated (e.g., no token-weighted SFT control). The 'largest corpus' claim is established only via a small comparison table.

Minor clarity issues: Figure 1's right panel lacks axis labels/values readability, the mapping of textual reward sub-weights (wd, wc, wl, wt, wlbl) to the five evaluation dimensions is implicit, and there is no error bar or seed variance reported for main results.

strengths: Substantial empirical contribution: the 3M chart-code pair corpus derived from real arXiv tables is the largest resource of its kind for chart-to-code generation, and the paper carefully documents its construction, filtering, and chart-type distribution (Table A, Figures G-I).

The SFT scaling analysis across six data sizes (200k to 2.8M) is a useful and honest empirical contribution that establishes a saturated SFT baseline, making the claimed RL gains more credible than in prior work that applies RL directly after weak SFT.

Comprehensive ablations are provided beyond the minimum: visual evaluator choice with human-score correlation (Figure A, Table B), GRPO vs. DPO (Table C), dataset comparison (Table D), reward-component and two-stage curriculum ablations with GPU-hour accounting (Table 5), and out-of-domain generalization to Seaborn/Plotly (Table 6).
Strong final results: the 7B model approaches GPT-4o on ChartMimic and ReachQA, with detailed low-level metric breakdowns (Table 3) rather than only aggregate scores.
Reproducibility statement and appendix are relatively complete, including exact prompts for data generation, quality filtering, and the visual reward, plus implementation hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core recipe combines well-established components already present in the literature: rule-based RLVR rewards (DeepSeekMath), rendering-based visual feedback (Rodriguez et al. 2025b; Gu et al. 2025, which the paper itself cites), and GRPO. The two-stage textual-then-visual curriculum is a sensible engineering choice, but there is no genuinely new technical insight; the contribution is largely an application/integration paper.

The visual reward relies on Qwen2.5-VL-72B as an LLM-as-judge for a student model of the same model family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), creating a self-preference/reward-hacking risk. The validator study (Figure A) is based on only 200 samples, and the paper provides no evidence of reward-hacking dynamics over the full RL run (e.g., divergence between visual reward and human-judged quality over training).

Headline framing is somewhat inconsistent with the ablations: Table 5 shows single-stage visual reward (V,-) achieving the best high-level score (84.01) and (T,T+V) with 22k+11k samples reaching 83.81 at 912 GPU hours, while the reported final numbers (83.8) match the cheaper 5.5k configuration. The 'two-stage strategy' is thus justified mainly by cost, not performance, which slightly weakens the central narrative.

Dataset quality is difficult to verify. All 3M pairs are generated by Gemini-2.5-Flash from extracted tables, with only execution-based and heuristic filtering; no public release or licensing discussion of the dataset is evident (the 'Project:' field on the title page is empty), which limits reproducibility and reuse of the paper's most significant resource.

Attribution of gains is muddied: the same Qwen2.5-VL-7B base is used throughout, but the paper does not disentangle how much improvement comes from the dataset scale/quality versus the RL strategy; Table 4's RL-only row uses only textual rewards and conflates baseline unsaturation with reward design.

Writing and presentation issues: an empty 'Project:' field on the title page, cluttered and hard-to-read figures (e.g., Figure 1 axis values, Figure 3 small reward curves), and no discussion of computational cost for the 60-GPU-hour SFT stage on 16 H800s relative to baselines, which complicates fair comparison with ChartCoder and others trained with fewer resources.

The 'SFT plateau' analysis, while empirically clean, is itself unsurprising and essentially restates known behavior of SFT scaling; the conceptual framing of this as a discovery overstates the insight.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: the paper systematically investigates SFT data scaling (200k to 2.8M samples) to establish a saturated SFT baseline, which is a methodologically sound way to isolate the true contribution of RL rather than comparing against an unsaturated SFT baseline (a common flaw in prior chart-to-code RL work).

Strong empirical results: MSRL achieves state-of-the-art performance on ChartMimic and ReachQA among open-source models, surpassing ChartCoder and rivaling GPT-4o, with a 7B model. The low-level metric breakdown (Table 3) is a nice addition.

Largest chart-to-code training corpus to date (3M pairs) built from real-world arXiv tables rather than purely synthetic sources, with a clear two-stage curation pipeline and a comparison table against prior datasets (Table 1).

Multi-granularity reward design is well-motivated: rule-based textual rewards for fine-grained code details plus an MLLM-based visual reward for global chart structure, with a two-stage curriculum justified by compute-efficiency trade-offs.

Unusually thorough ablations: SFT/RL interplay (Table 4), reward type combinations with GPU-hour costs (Table 5), visual evaluator choice validated against human scores with Pearson correlation analysis (Figure A, Table B), GRPO vs DPO (Table C), dataset ablation (Table D), and out-of-distribution generalization to Seaborn/Plotly (Table 6).

Good reproducibility practices: full implementation details (hyperparameters, reward weights, GPU hours), prompt templates in the appendix, and a reproducibility statement with code in supplementary materials.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core recipe (GRPO + rule-based verifiable rewards + LLM-as-judge visual reward + two-stage curriculum) assembles well-known components from DeepSeek-R1-style RLVR, MMEureka, Chart-R1, and rendering-aware RL (e.g., Rodriguez et al. 2025b for vector graphics). The contribution is primarily an empirical/application one within the chart-to-code niche.

Possible reward-model bias: the visual reward uses Qwen2.5-VL-72B, the same model family as the base policy (Qwen2.5-VL-7B). While the evaluator ablation partially addresses this, the paper does not quantify reward hacking over the course of training, and the human-validated sample (200 instances, 100 manual checks) is small.

Confounded comparisons: MSRL-SFT is trained on 2.8M samples while compared chart-domain models (e.g., ChartCoder at 115k) use far less data, so part of the SOTA margin reflects data scale rather than method. Table D partially mitigates this but is limited to ChartCoder's dataset.

Benchmark coverage is narrow: evaluation is restricted to ChartMimic and ReachQA, both matplotlib-centric; Plot2Code and other chart-to-code benchmarks are not evaluated, weakening generalization claims beyond the training distribution (the Seaborn/Plotly test is small: 107 and 150 examples).

Data quality concerns: the 3M corpus is generated by Gemini-2.5-Flash from tables, and RL data is filtered from the same distribution; the paper does not report a human audit of the large SFT corpus, and potential correlation between the generation pipeline and benchmark styles is not analyzed.

The two-stage strategy is not clearly optimal: in Table 5, single-stage visual-only reward achieves the best Low-Level (79.13) and High-Level (84.01) scores, yet the paper adopts the two-stage configuration mainly for compute reasons; the main reported results thus trade some performance for efficiency, which should be stated more explicitly.
No variance reporting: results appear to be from single runs without multiple seeds or significance tests, which matters given gaps of 1-2 points between some configurations.

Minor presentation issues: reward-weight notation is overloaded (wt used for both textual weight in Eq. 1 and title weight in the textual reward), Figure 1's y-axes are truncated in a potentially misleading way, and the abstract's improvement claims (+6.2%/+9.9%) mix metrics without specifying exact baselines.
